scale_010:n1.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the setup of our new data warehouse using {{vendor}}. This is step 1 of standing up our data warehouse & BI stack, and it requires my explicit sign-off before anything is applied.

First, ask me for any missing inputs: our {{vendor}} account/organization name (or confirm we need to create one), the cloud region we want data hosted in, the list of production systems and file formats (CSV/JSON/Parquet/Iceberg/Delta) we'll need to load or query, and which BI tool (Metabase) will connect for dashboards.

Then, using your configured credentials, prepare a complete setup plan and draft configuration for {{vendor}}:
- Draft the initial warehouse/compute sizing and naming.
- Identify and list the first-party/partner connectors needed for our named sources (SaaS apps, databases, ETL/ELT tools), noting documented setup steps for each.
- Draft the bulk-load approach for CSV/JSON/Parquet from our cloud object storage using the documented single-command load method.
- Note how to enable managed continuous ingestion for new files/events, and how to query open table formats (Iceberg/Delta/Parquet) directly in object storage without pre-loading.
- Note the streaming ingestion option if we need near-real-time data.
- Draft the JDBC/ODBC connection details and role/security configuration needed for Metabase to connect.
- Prepare a checklist of all roles, users, and permissions that will be created, clearly flagging any security-sensitive settings.

Do NOT create the account, provision the warehouse, assign roles, or apply any security/role configuration yourself — this step carries data-governance risk and must stop for human sign-off. Compile everything into a single clear summary document with all drafted values, connector list, and the security/role checklist, and present it to me for review and approval before any changes are applied.

scale_010:n2.prompt:
You are helping me configure {{vendor}} (our customer data platform) to collect production events for our data warehouse & BI stack, ahead of a required human approval before anything goes live.

Please do the following:
1. Ask me for: our {{vendor}} workspace/account details, which production systems (web, mobile, server apps, or third-party cloud apps/feeds) should send events, and the destination warehouse (Snowflake or BigQuery) already configured.
2. Using {{vendor}}'s documented API or MCP server (using your configured credentials), draft the event source configuration: define the sources to create, the tracking spec fields (track, identify, page) each source should emit, and how server-side events will be sent via the HTTP ingestion API (e.g. POST /v1/events) with proper authentication and delivery guarantees.
3. For any official SDKs needed on web/mobile/server apps, prepare the integration snippets and note where they'd be added in our codebase, but do not commit or deploy code changes yourself.
4. For third-party cloud apps/feeds, identify which connectors {{vendor}} supports and prepare the connection settings (without submitting/activating them).
5. Compile a clear checklist showing: sources to be created, streams/destinations to be wired, expected event volume, and how deliveries will be inspected/verified post-launch.
6. Do NOT create sources, activate streams, or send live events to {{vendor}} — only prepare drafts and configuration plans.

When finished, report back with: the full draft configuration (sources, SDK snippets, ingestion API usage, third-party connectors), the verification/checklist plan, and any open questions needing my input. Then stop for human sign-off — I will review and explicitly approve before anything is applied in {{vendor}}.

scale_010:n3.prompt:
You are helping me draft the data models for our new data warehouse, which will run on Snowflake or BigQuery (ask me which one we're using, plus my production system sources like Postgres/MySQL/app databases, and any known reporting needs) with Metabase for dashboards. Please do NOT execute any DDL or apply changes to the warehouse — this step is design-only.

Actions:
1. Ask me for: the target warehouse (Snowflake or BigQuery), a list of production source systems/tables I want modeled, and the key business questions or reports we want Metabase to answer.
2. Propose a warehouse schema design following standard practice: staging layer (raw ingested tables mirroring source systems), a core/warehouse layer (cleaned, conformed dimension and fact tables using star-schema or similar), and any mart/aggregate tables needed for the reporting use cases I described.
3. For each proposed table, document: table name, layer, grain, key columns, data types, and relationships (primary/foreign keys) in plain text or markdown.
4. Draft the corresponding CREATE TABLE SQL statements for the target warehouse's SQL dialect, clearly labeled as drafts.
5. Note any assumptions, open questions, or missing source information you need me to clarify.
6. Compile everything into a single design document (schema diagram description in words, table list, SQL drafts, open questions) and present it to me for review.

Done looks like: a complete draft data model document with staging, core, and mart layer definitions, draft SQL for each table, and a list of assumptions/questions — with nothing yet applied to any live warehouse.

Report back with the full draft document, a summary of key modeling decisions, and any open questions. Then stop for human sign-off before any of these models are created or applied in Snowflake/BigQuery.

scale_010:n4.prompt:
You are helping me connect our Customer Data Platform, {{vendor}}, to our data warehouse as part of standing up our BI stack. Before starting, ask me for anything missing: which warehouse we use (Snowflake or BigQuery), the warehouse name/schema where {{vendor}} should land data, my {{vendor}} workspace/account details, and confirmation of which production event sources and destinations need to be wired.

Using {{vendor}}'s documented API or MCP server (and your configured credentials), please prepare a complete connection plan and, where the tooling allows, stage the configuration without activating it live:
1. Define the warehouse destination in {{vendor}} (host, database, schema, target tables) so raw events/profiles land on a schedule I control.
2. Configure or list the source streams that should route into the warehouse, with per-destination field mapping and any filtering rules.
3. If {{vendor}} supports warehouse-native modeling/reverse ETL, draft the model/audience definitions that would run against existing warehouse tables rather than re-collecting data.
4. If the integration exposes a warehouse query capability (e.g., a Jitsu Function using ctx.getWarehouse(...)) note where that could be used to validate delivered data.
5. Produce a checklist summarizing: sources wired, destination schema/tables, mapping/filtering rules, sync schedule, and any warehouse-native audience definitions staged.

Do not activate the pipeline, trigger real data syncs, or make the connection live — a human must explicitly approve before changes are applied. Stop for human sign-off once the plan and staged configuration are ready, and present the checklist plus any open questions for my review and approval.

scale_010:n5.prompt:
You are helping me verify that data pipelines feeding my data warehouse (Snowflake or BigQuery — ask me which one I'm using if not already known) are running correctly and that Metabase dashboards are reflecting fresh data. This is an async check: pipeline runs happen on a schedule, so you must poll/verify status rather than assume a single check is final.

First, ask me for: (1) which warehouse I use (Snowflake or BigQuery), (2) which pipeline/ELT tool moves data from production systems into it (e.g. Fivetran, Airbyte, custom scripts), (3) the names of the key source tables/schemas I expect to see populated, (4) expected sync frequency, and (5) the Metabase dashboard(s) or questions that depend on this data.

Then, using my configured credentials, do the following:
1. Check the pipeline tool's sync/run history or logs to confirm the most recent run(s) completed successfully and note timestamps.
2. Query the warehouse (via its console/API) to confirm the expected tables exist, have recent rows (compare row counts or max timestamp to expected freshness), and show no obvious gaps or duplicates.
3. Open or query the relevant Metabase dashboard(s)/questions to confirm they load without errors and show data consistent with what you found in the warehouse.
4. If anything is stale, failed, or missing, capture the specific error message, table name, and timestamp.

Done looks like: a clear pass/fail report per pipeline and per dashboard, including last successful sync time, row/freshness check results, and any errors found. Report back with a short table summarizing each source system → warehouse table → last sync status → Metabase dashboard status, plus any recommended next action for failures. Note explicitly which parts you were able to verify now versus which require a later re-check due to pipeline scheduling.

scale_010:n6.prompt:
You are helping me set up Metabase dashboards on top of our data warehouse as part of standing up our BI stack. Before starting, ask me for any of the following you don't already have: (1) our Metabase instance URL and confirmation that it's reachable, (2) the warehouse type (Snowflake or BigQuery) and the specific database/schema/tables the dashboards should query, (3) which business questions or metrics we want visualized (e.g. signups, revenue, churn, pipeline health), (4) who should have access to which dashboards (roles/groups), and (5) any existing dashboard/collection naming conventions.

Using your configured credentials, connect to the Metabase instance and: verify or configure the data source connection to our warehouse (using the connection details I provide, not by inventing any), organize dashboards into a logical collection structure, draft the specific questions/queries and chart types needed for each requested metric, and lay out draft dashboards grouping related questions together. Document proposed data source settings, collection structure, each question's underlying query logic (in plain words, not SQL you invent independently — confirm query intent with me if ambiguous), and access/permission settings for each dashboard.

Done looks like: a written plan showing the data source configuration, dashboard/collection structure, each dashboard's questions with their purpose, and the proposed access permissions — all staged as drafts in Metabase but not yet published or shared with end users.

Do not connect any new data source, publish any dashboard, or change any permissions live until I review. Report back with the full draft plan and a summary of what would be created/changed, then stop for human sign-off before applying any changes.

scale_010:n7.prompt:
You are helping me prepare an executive dashboard in Metabase, connected to our data warehouse (Snowflake or BigQuery, whichever we already have configured). This is an 'assist' step: you should prepare everything but a human executive must review and approve the metric selection before anything is finalized.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already clear: our Metabase URL, which warehouse we use (Snowflake or BigQuery), the schema/table names for key production data (revenue, customers, usage, pipeline, etc.), and any existing dashboards or metrics leadership has previously flagged as important.

Then do the following:
1. Using your configured credentials, connect to Metabase and review available data sources/tables in the warehouse.
2. Draft a proposed list of 8-12 candidate executive metrics (e.g., MRR, churn, active users, pipeline value, burn rate) with a one-line rationale for each, based on what data is actually available.
3. For each candidate metric, draft the underlying query or Metabase question definition and a suggested chart type (trend line, KPI card, funnel, etc.), but do not save them as final dashboard content yet.
4. Assemble a draft dashboard layout proposal (which cards, grouping, order) as a mockup/description, and create it in Metabase as a draft/unpublished dashboard if the tool supports that state.
5. Prepare a short summary document listing the proposed metrics, their definitions, data sources, and open questions (e.g., ambiguous metric definitions, missing data).

Done looks like: a draft dashboard exists in Metabase with clearly labeled draft status, plus a written summary of proposed metrics and rationale ready for executive review.

Do not publish, share broadly, or mark the dashboard as final — this requires leadership to choose which metrics reflect real business priorities. Stop for human sign-off once the draft and summary are ready, and report back what you built, what decisions are pending, and any data gaps you found.
